title: Design a key-value store (Dynamo-style)
scopeHtml: Scope: partitioning, replication, quorums, vector clocks, hinted handoff, anti-entropy, LSM storage.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A key-value store maps a key to a value: put(key, value) and get(key). A Dynamo-style store does this across many machines, always writable, and tolerates failures. Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007) inspired Cassandra, Riak and DynamoDB. The shopping cart is the classic use: never refuse an "add to cart".

Functional

  • put(key, value), get(key), delete(key).
  • Values are opaque blobs, small (under 1 MB, typically 1 to 10 KB).
  • Optional: TTL, conditional writes.

Non-functional

  • Highly available for writes (no single leader that blocks writes).
  • Horizontally scalable: add nodes, data rebalances.
  • Low latency: p99 under 10 ms.
  • Tunable consistency (eventual by default, stronger when requested).
  • Survives node, rack and even data-centre failure.

Decision gravity. The big choice is CAP: Dynamo picks availability over strict consistency (AP). That is a one-way door for the data model: if you later need strong cross-key transactions you need a different system (Spanner, a relational DB). Reversible within the system by tuning quorum per request.

Everyday analogy. A phone book copied into three offices; any office can add a number, and they sync up later.

Common interview traps.

  • Not stating CAP preference and consistency model.
  • Proposing a single master and calling it highly available.
  • Confusing this with a cache (it must be durable).

notes.title: API
notes.html:
PUT /v1/kv/{key}
Headers: X-Consistency: quorum | one | all   (optional, default quorum)
         If-Match: <version-context>          (optional, for read-modify-write)
{ "value": "<base64 bytes>", "ttlSeconds": 86400 }

200 OK
{ "version": "[(nodeA,3),(nodeB,1)]" }       // vector clock context
503 Service Unavailable -> could not reach enough replicas
GET /v1/kv/{key}?consistency=quorum
200 OK  { "values": [ {"value": "<b64>", "context": "[(A,3),(B,1)]"} ] }
// More than one entry in "values" means conflicting siblings: the client merges.
404 Not Found
DELETE /v1/kv/{key}   -> 204 (writes a tombstone)

Client-side library does the real work: it knows the ring, picks a coordinator and retries. Internal node-to-node RPCs: replicate(key, value, clock), read(key), hint(key, value, forNode), gossip(state), merkleRoot(range).

Industry example. DynamoDB exposes PutItem/GetItem with ConsistentRead flag; Cassandra exposes consistency levels ONE, QUORUM, ALL per query.

Everyday analogy. A form where you tick "tell me when 2 of the 3 offices have it".

Common interview traps.

  • Not exposing what happens on conflicts (siblings, last-write-wins).
  • Forgetting deletes need tombstones in an eventually consistent store.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 10B keys, average value 1 KB, replication factor N = 3, 200k ops/s peak (80% reads).

Quantity Calculation Result
Raw data 10B x 1 KB 10 TB
With replicas x3 30 TB
Per node (say 2 TB usable, 50% headroom) 30 TB / 1 TB used ~30 nodes
Write rate 40k/s x 3 replicas 120k replica writes/s
Per node 120k / 30 ~4k writes/s plus reads, easy for SSD + LSM
Index memory (bloom + index) ~10 bits per key per node 10B x 3 x 10 bits / 8 = ~37 GB total, ~1.2 GB/node

Start with 36 nodes in 3 racks for headroom. Disk is the constraint, not CPU.

Everyday analogy. Working out how many filing cabinets you need if every file is stored in three copies.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the replication factor in storage.
  • Ignoring compaction headroom (LSM needs 30 to 50% free disk).

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Building blocks (the Dynamo toolbox)

  1. Partitioning: consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes.
  2. Replication: each key stored on the next N nodes clockwise on the ring (the preference list).
  3. Consistency: quorums: W writes + R reads with R + W > N.
  4. Versioning: vector clocks to detect conflicting writes.
  5. Failure handling: sloppy quorum plus hinted handoff for temporary failures; Merkle trees for repair.
  6. Membership: gossip protocol, no central master.
  7. Storage engine per node: LSM tree (memtable, WAL, SSTables).

Any node can be the coordinator (client picks via the ring or any node forwards). No single point of failure.

Decision gravity. Leaderless replication is the foundational choice: great availability, harder consistency. Alternative: single leader per partition (Raft, as in CockroachDB/Spanner/etcd), which gives linearizability but pauses writes during leader election. Choice is effectively a one-way door.

Industry examples. Cassandra and Riak copy the design; DynamoDB (the managed service) is Dynamo-inspired but internally uses leader-based Multi-Paxos per partition. Voldemort powered LinkedIn.

Everyday analogy. A team with no manager: anyone can take an order, and teammates tell each other the news.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "like Redis cluster" (that has primaries and replicas, a different model).
  • Not mentioning virtual nodes.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Partitioning with consistent hashing

Hash the key (MD5/Murmur3) onto a ring 0 to 2^128. Each node owns the arc before it. Adding a node moves only about 1/N of keys, not all (modulo hashing would move almost everything).

Virtual nodes: each physical node takes 128 to 256 random points on the ring, so load is even and a failed node's data spreads over many neighbours instead of one. Heterogeneous machines take more vnodes.

Worked example: 36 nodes x 256 vnodes = 9,216 ring points; losing one node redistributes its ~1/36 over many peers (about 2.8% of data), not onto a single neighbour.

Decision gravity. Partition key and hash function are one-way: changing them rewrites all data. Number of vnodes is easy to tune early, painful later.

Replication and quorums

N = 3 replicas. A write succeeds after W acks, a read waits for R responses; R + W > N guarantees the read overlaps the latest write.

Config Behaviour
N=3, W=2, R=2 Balanced default, tolerates 1 failure
W=1, R=3 Fast writes, slow reads
W=3, R=1 Fast reads, writes fail if any node is down
W=1, R=1 Fastest, eventual consistency only

Coordinator sends to all 3 and replies when 2 ack. Quorum does not equal linearizability: sloppy quorums, clock issues and concurrent writes can still return stale data.

Conflicts and vector clocks

Two clients update the same cart at the same time on different replicas. Which wins? A vector clock is a list of (node, counter) pairs attached to each version.

v1: [(A,1)]                   cart = {milk}
v2: [(A,2)]                   cart = {milk, eggs}      descends from v1
v3: [(A,1),(B,1)]             cart = {milk, bread}     concurrent with v2

v2 supersedes v1 (counters all greater or equal). v2 and v3 are concurrent: neither contains the other, so both are returned as siblings and the application merges (union of carts). Alternative: last-write-wins by timestamp (Cassandra default): simple but silently drops writes and relies on synced clocks. For counters/sets use CRDTs.

Vector clocks grow with the number of writers; Dynamo truncates old entries (a rare loss of precision).

Handling failures: sloppy quorum and hinted handoff

If a replica is down, write to the next healthy node on the ring with a hint ("this belongs to node C"). When C returns, the holder hands the data back. This keeps writes available during failures at the cost of temporary inconsistency. Hints expire (for example 3 hours); longer outages need repair.

Anti-entropy with Merkle trees

Replicas drift. Each node keeps a Merkle tree (a hash tree) per key range. Two replicas compare root hashes; if equal, in sync; if not, descend to find the differing leaves and sync only those. Cuts repair traffic from comparing billions of keys to a few hash exchanges. Cassandra runs nodetool repair for this and recommends it at least within gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days).

Membership and failure detection

No central master. Each node gossips its view of the cluster to a few random peers every second. Failure detection uses a phi-accrual detector (Cassandra) rather than a fixed timeout. New nodes contact seed nodes to join.

Storage engine: LSM tree

  1. Append to the commit log (WAL) for durability, then insert into the in-memory memtable.
  2. When the memtable reaches ~64 MB, flush to an immutable sorted SSTable.
  3. Reads check memtable, then SSTables newest first, using Bloom filters to skip files that definitely lack the key.
  4. Background compaction merges SSTables, drops overwritten values and expired tombstones.

Why LSM: sequential writes are fast (write-heavy workloads). Cost: read amplification and compaction I/O (write amplification 10x+). B-trees (as in DynamoDB's older designs, Postgres) read well but write randomly.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: read latency climbs over days and disk fills. Metric: pending compactions and SSTable count per read. Cause: compaction falling behind or tombstone buildup. Fix: more compaction throughput, avoid delete-heavy patterns, repair on schedule.

Reads: read repair

When a quorum read sees different versions, the coordinator returns the newest and asynchronously writes it to stale replicas ("read repair"), so frequently read data heals itself.

Everyday analogy. Vector clocks are like two people editing a shared recipe on paper: if neither saw the other's edit, you need a human to merge them.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing R + W > N gives strong consistency in all cases.
  • Using LWW without admitting lost updates.
  • Forgetting tombstones, so deleted data comes back from a stale replica ("zombie data").
  • Hot keys: one celebrity key overloads its 3 replicas; mitigate with caching or key splitting.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Explicit CAP position and consistency knobs (N, R, W).
  • The full toolbox: consistent hashing with vnodes, quorums, vector clocks, hinted handoff, Merkle trees, gossip.
  • Why each exists: availability during failures, convergence afterwards.
  • Storage engine understanding (LSM, WAL, bloom filters, compaction).
  • Conflict resolution strategy and its cost (siblings vs LWW vs CRDT).
  • Capacity numbers and rack/data-centre awareness (replicas on different racks and DCs).
  • Seniors discuss hot partitions, rebalancing speed, cross-DC replication latency, tombstone/GC settings and compare with leader-based systems (Raft, Spanner).

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting Dynamo terms with no numbers or failure story.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Dynamo-style = leaderless, AP, always-writable KV store with tunable consistency.
  • Partition by consistent hashing with virtual nodes; replicate to the next N nodes (N=3, different racks).
  • Quorums (R + W > N) tune the latency/consistency trade; sloppy quorum + hinted handoff keep writes available.
  • Vector clocks detect concurrent writes; app merges siblings, or accept last-write-wins and lost updates.
  • Merkle trees and read repair converge replicas; gossip handles membership.
  • Per-node storage is an LSM tree (WAL, memtable, SSTable, bloom filter, compaction).
  • Choosing leaderless AP is a one-way door; quorum levels are per-request tunable.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a distributed key-value store use consistent hashing with virtual nodes instead of hash(key) % N?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic building block; they want to see you understand rebalancing cost and load spread.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With modulo, changing N remaps almost every key, so adding a node causes a massive data shuffle. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. Virtual nodes (128 to 256 points per physical node) even out the load and spread a failed node's data across many peers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Hash key (Murmur3/MD5) onto 0..2^128. Each node owns the arc before its position.
  • Without vnodes, one random position per node gives uneven arcs; a failed node dumps all its data on its single neighbour.
  • With 36 nodes x 256 vnodes = 9,216 points, losing a node redistributes about 1/36 (2.8%) over many peers.
  • Heterogeneous machines get more vnodes in proportion to capacity.
Key hash -> Node A (owner) -> Node B (replica 2) -> Node C (replica 3)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "consistent hashing" without vnodes.
  • Putting replica 2 and 3 on vnodes of the same physical node or same rack.
  • Treating the partition key and hash as changeable later.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are partition key and hash function a one-way door? -> Changing them rewrites all data.
  2. How do you place replicas? -> Next N distinct physical nodes clockwise, spread across racks and data centres.
  3. What about a hot key? -> Ring placement does not help; cache it or split the key.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "only 1/N keys move". The senior covers vnodes, rack-aware replica choice and which decisions are irreversible.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cluster without vnodes lost one node and its single neighbour went from 60% to 100% disk, taking it down too.

questions.promptHtml: With N=3, W=2, R=2, do you get strong consistency? How are conflicting concurrent writes detected and resolved?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the common misconception that R + W > N means linearizability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: R + W > N guarantees that read and write sets overlap, so a read sees at least one replica with the latest acknowledged write, but it is not linearizability: sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, clock skew and failed partial writes can still produce stale or conflicting reads. Concurrent writes are detected with vector clocks, and resolved by the application merging siblings, by last-write-wins (simple but loses writes) or by CRDTs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Config Behaviour
N=3, W=2, R=2 Balanced; tolerates 1 failure
W=1, R=3 Fast writes, slow reads
W=3, R=1 Fast reads, writes fail if any node is down
W=1, R=1 Fastest, eventual only 
v1: [(A,1)]            cart = {milk}
v2: [(A,2)]            cart = {milk, eggs}     descends from v1
v3: [(A,1),(B,1)]      cart = {milk, bread}    concurrent with v2

v2 supersedes v1; v2 and v3 are concurrent, so both are returned as siblings and the app unions them. Vector clocks grow with writers; Dynamo truncates old entries.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming R + W > N is strong consistency.
  • LWW without admitting silent write loss and clock dependence.
  • Forgetting tombstones for deletes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a quorum read still be stale? -> A sloppy quorum wrote to hint nodes outside the preference list, so a later read quorum may not include them.
  2. What does Cassandra do by default? -> Last-write-wins by timestamp.
  3. When use CRDTs? -> Counters, sets, where merge is defined mathematically.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "R+W>N gives consistency". Senior: names the limits, the vector clock ordering rule and the cost of each conflict strategy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used LWW for shopping carts and lost items when two devices updated simultaneously.

questions.contextHtml: Design the cluster for 10B keys, 1 KB average value, RF=3, peak 200k ops/s with 80% reads, p99 under 10 ms. Nodes have 2 TB usable SSD. The interviewer says "give me a node count and tell me what the constraint is."
questions.promptHtml: Do the math and size the cluster.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Forgets replication or compaction headroom, or says "CPU is the limit".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 1 KB the average or p99? Compression expected? Are values mutable (compaction churn)? Multi-DC?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Disk capacity is the binding constraint; writes are modest.
  4. How I'd verify each: Raw data 10B x 1 KB = 10 TB; x3 = 30 TB. LSM needs 30 to 50% free for compaction, so about 1 TB used per 2 TB node: 30 nodes. Write rate: 40k/s x 3 = 120k replica writes/s, about 4k per node. Index: bloom plus index about 10 bits per key per replica: 10B x 3 x 10 bits / 8 = about 37 GB total, about 1.2 GB per node.
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix: Start with 36 nodes across 3 racks for headroom, 256 vnodes each, RF=3 with one replica per rack. 200k ops/s over 36 nodes is about 5.5k per node, easy for SSD plus LSM.
  7. Prevention: Alert at 60% disk; track pending compactions; plan expansion before 70%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not size for 100% disk fill; compaction can double space temporarily.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compression 2x? -> Halves the disk, but I keep the headroom rule and verify with real data.
  • Values are 100 KB? -> Different system: store blobs in object storage, pointer in the KV.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cluster sized at 85% disk could not finish a major compaction and went read-only.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no replication factor in storage.
  • Hire: 30 TB and headroom to about 30-36 nodes.
  • Strong hire: index memory, rack spread, headroom rationale.

questions.contextHtml:
Users report deleted records coming back. A node was down for 12 days during a data-centre issue and rejoined yesterday. Config: gc_grace_seconds = 10 days, repairs not run on schedule for that range.

nodetool status: node7 UN (back 20h ago)
read key=user:991 CL=ONE -> returns deleted record (from node7)
read key=user:991 CL=QUORUM -> returns record on 1 of 3, tombstone on 2 of 3 -> deleted

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cache problem" or "replication is broken", with no mention of tombstones.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which read consistency? When did node7 go down relative to the deletes? Is repair automated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise read consistency for sensitive paths to QUORUM; run repair on node7's ranges immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Node7 missed the deletes; the other replicas already purged the tombstones after gc_grace_seconds so node7's old data would now resurrect.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check dates of the deletes vs node downtime; look at SSTable tombstone metadata; nodetool repair logs.
  5. Root cause: A delete in an eventually consistent store is a tombstone write. If a replica is down longer than the tombstone grace period, other replicas drop the tombstone and the stale replica reintroduces the data.
  6. Fix: Short term: repair right away (before tombstones are purged, if still possible) or wipe and rebootstrap node7. Long term: scheduled repairs within gc_grace_seconds; do not bring back a node down longer than the grace period without wipe or repair.
  7. Prevention: Repair scheduler with alerts on missed windows; an ops rule on dead-node age.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shorten gc_grace_seconds as a fix: it increases zombie risk. I would not rely on read repair alone for cold data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Delete-heavy workload? -> Tombstone buildup slows reads; use TTLs or time-bucketed tables.
  • Merkle tree repair cost? -> Compare range hashes, then stream only the differing leaves.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Deleted GDPR records resurfaced after a replaced node was brought back with old disks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no tombstone concept.
  • Hire: explains grace period and repair.
  • Strong hire: gives operational rule, wipe/rebootstrap and monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: Two teams want to use the store. Team A runs a shopping cart: "never refuse an add-to-cart". Team B runs account balances for a wallet and wants "no double-spend, ever". Both ask if they can use the same cluster with the same settings (N=3, W=1, R=1).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Same settings for both" or "use QUORUM and it is strongly consistent".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can Team B tolerate unavailability during partitions? Does the wallet need cross-key transactions (transfer A to B)? What is the cost of a stale cart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cart fits AP; wallet needs linearizable single-key and likely multi-key transactions, which a leaderless AP store does not give.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write down invariants: cart is mergeable (set union); balance is not (concurrent debits conflict).
  5. Root cause: Different consistency requirements.
  6. Fix: Cart: W=2, R=2 or even W=1, with siblings merged by set union. Wallet: a leader-based system (Raft or Spanner-like, or a relational DB) with transactions; if forced on this store, use conditional writes plus quorum, but I would still call it risky.
  7. Prevention: A data classification doc listing consistency needs per dataset.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use R+W>N as a substitute for transactions. Leaderless AP is a one-way door for the data model; moving a wallet later is costly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Unique usernames? -> Needs consensus; use a lightweight transaction or a separate strongly consistent service.
  • Per-request tuning? -> Yes, consistency level is selectable per call.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A loyalty-points balance on an AP store drifted by double-spends under network partitions; moving it to a consensus-backed DB ended the reconciliation job.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one config for all.
  • Hire: AP for cart, CP for wallet.
  • Strong hire: ties to invariants, merge semantics and one-way door.

questions.contextHtml:
During a flash sale, one product key product:777 gets 60k reads/s. The three replicas holding it show CPU 98%, p99 latency 450 ms, while the other 33 nodes are at 20%.

node11 cpu 98%  reads/s 20,100  p99 430ms
node19 cpu 97%  reads/s 19,800
node27 cpu 98%  reads/s 20,000
others cpu ~20%

Someone suggests adding more nodes to the cluster.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do now and what is the long-term design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add nodes; increase RF to 36.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it one key? Is the value read-mostly? Can it be stale for a few seconds?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a cache in front (app-local cache or CDN for the product) with a short TTL; temporarily route this key's reads with consistency ONE.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Single hot key bound to 3 replicas; compaction contention; GC pauses.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-key hit metrics, node CPU skew, nodetool toppartitions (Cassandra) or equivalent.
  5. Root cause: A key maps to exactly N replicas, so adding nodes does not add capacity for it.
  6. Fix: Cache with a short TTL at the client or edge; key splitting (product:777#0..#7) for hot read-only data with reads choosing a random suffix; for writes hot keys use counters per shard merged on read.
  7. Prevention: Hot key detector; load tests with a Zipf distribution; per-key rate limits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Key splitting makes updates fan out and temporarily inconsistent across copies; acceptable for catalog data. I would not raise RF to everything.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The hot key is written often? -> Buffer or aggregate writes, or CRDT counters.
  • Read repair adding load? -> Lower read repair chance for that table.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A celebrity profile key saturated three replicas while the cluster was 80% idle; a client-side cache cut 95% of the load.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: add nodes.
  • Hire: cache plus key splitting.
  • Strong hire: explains why capacity cannot scale per key and the trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
Read p99 climbed from 6 ms to 70 ms over 5 days. Disk usage rose from 55% to 88%.

pending compactions: 1,840 (was 12)
sstables per read (p99): 34 (was 4)
compaction throughput limit: 16 MB/s
write rate: 3x higher since a backfill job started 6 days ago
tombstone scans per read: 9,000 on table events_by_user

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add RAM" or "restart nodes".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What started 6 days ago? Is the backfill still running? Is disk full imminent? Do we delete heavily?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle or pause the backfill; raise compaction throughput (for example from 16 to 128 MB/s) while watching I/O latency.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Compaction falling behind write rate; tombstone buildup from deletes; a bad compaction strategy for the workload.
  4. How I'd verify each: Pending compactions, sstables per read, tombstone warnings, disk throughput vs limits.
  5. Root cause: The backfill tripled writes, compaction at 16 MB/s could not keep up, SSTable count rose so each read checked many files (read amplification); tombstones made scans slow.
  6. Fix: Short term: throttle backfill, raise compactor throughput, add temporary nodes if disk is near 90%. Long term: capacity for 3x write bursts, time-window compaction for time-series, TTLs instead of deletes, scheduled repair.
  7. Prevention: Alert on pending compactions and sstables per read; free disk 30 to 50% rule.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Raising compaction throughput steals disk I/O from reads; I would do it gradually. I would not run a manual full compaction at 88% disk: it needs temporary space.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Write amplification of LSM? -> Often 10x or more; it is the price for sequential writes.
  • Bloom filters? -> Skip SSTables that cannot contain the key; false positives still cost reads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A backfill without a rate limit pushed disks to 90% and compaction could no longer run; the fix was throttling plus emergency capacity.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts nodes.
  • Hire: ties lag to compaction and write rate.
  • Strong hire: tombstones, compaction strategy, headroom and throttled recovery.

questions.contextHtml: Rack 2 loses power. Three nodes are down for 4 hours; the rack comes back. Meanwhile coordinators used sloppy quorums and hinted handoff. Hints expire after 3 hours. Writes continued at 40k/s during the outage. The interviewer asks how you bring the cluster back to full consistency without a customer-visible impact.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Nodes catch up on their own."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which consistency levels did clients use? How many hints were stored and how many expired? Is repair automated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Let nodes rejoin; keep serving at QUORUM; throttle repair streaming so it does not hurt p99.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hints delivered for the first 3 hours; writes in hour 4 are missing on those nodes; hints that had been dropped leave divergence.
  4. How I'd verify each: Hint backlog metrics, replica comparison through Merkle tree root hashes per range.
  5. Root cause: Hinted handoff is a best-effort short-term repair; long outages need anti-entropy.
  6. Fix: Run range-based repair on the three nodes: compare Merkle roots, descend to differing leaves, stream only those. Order: nodes with the most expired hints first. Read repair heals hot data in the meantime.
  7. Prevention: Rack-aware placement so one rack never holds all replicas of a key; scheduled repairs; alerts on hint expiry.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not run full repair at max speed during peak; it competes with live traffic. I would not extend hint windows indefinitely: unbounded hint storage hurts healthy nodes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A disk is lost permanently? -> Replace node, bootstrap by streaming its ranges from replicas, then repair.
  • Cross-DC? -> Local quorum reads and writes, async replication across DCs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a rack outage a team relied on hints alone and discovered missing writes a week later during a data audit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: assumes self-healing.
  • Hire: hints plus Merkle repair.
  • Strong hire: throttling, ordering, rack-aware placement and monitoring.
